sections.title: What is a Set? (Creation & Basics) — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Write a function that takes a list of student names (with duplicates
  from multiple class rosters) and returns:
  - Total entries (with duplicates)
  - Unique student count
  - Duplicate names (names that appeared more than once)
  - A cleaned list (duplicates removed, sorted alphabetically)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Build a "unique word counter" for a paragraph:
  - Split text into words (handle punctuation)
  - Store unique words in a set
  - Find words that appear in ALL of 3 different paragraphs
  - Find words unique to only one paragraph

CHALLENGE 3:
  Create a "social network mutual friends" system:
  - Each user has a set of friends
  - Find mutual friends between two users
  - Find people user A follows but B doesn't
  - Suggest friends (friends-of-friends not already followed)

CHALLENGE 4:
  Given a list of product orders (each order has a set of items),
  find:
  - Items ordered by ALL customers
  - Items ordered by at least one customer
  - Items ordered by exactly one customer
  - Most "exclusive" item (fewest customers)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Implement a duplicate file detector:
  - Given list of filenames with paths
  - Detect duplicate filenames (same name, different path)
  - Detect duplicate extensions
  - Return a report of all duplicates found

CHALLENGE 6:
  Build a "lottery number validator":
  - Valid ticket: 6 unique numbers between 1-49
  - Use sets to validate no duplicates
  - Check if a ticket is a winner (matches winning set)
  - Find how many numbers matched (partial wins)
  - Handle invalid inputs gracefully

CHALLENGE 7:
  Write a function that takes two sets of GPS coordinates
  (as tuples) representing delivery zones, and returns:
  - Coordinates in both zones (overlap)
  - Coordinates only in zone A
  - Coordinates only in zone B
  - Whether zones are completely separate (disjoint)
  - Whether one zone completely contains the other
```

sections.title: Set Properties Deep Dive — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Create a function that proves all 4 set properties with clear
  demonstrations:
  - Show unordered (run same set creation 5 times, check if order varies)
  - Show uniqueness (add 100 duplicates, check count)
  - Show mutability (add/remove and verify)
  - Show hashability (test 10 different types)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Implement a "type-safe set" class that:
  - Only accepts elements of one type (specified at creation)
  - Raises TypeError with helpful message for wrong types
  - Still supports all normal set operations
  - Has a type() method returning the accepted type

CHALLENGE 3:
  Write a function that takes any iterable and:
  - Returns count of unique elements
  - Returns count of duplicates
  - Returns which elements are duplicated (with count)
  - Returns the "duplication ratio" (duplicates/total)
  Handle nested lists by flattening first.

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "fingerprinting" system using sets:
  - Given a document (string), create its "fingerprint"
    as the set of unique words
  - Compare two documents' fingerprints for similarity
  - Return Jaccard similarity: |intersection| / |union|
  - Find documents with > 70% similarity

CHALLENGE 5:
  Demonstrate the True/1/1.0 and False/0 gotcha:
  - Create sets with various combinations of 1, True, 1.0, 0, False
  - Show what gets stored and why
  - Write a function that warns users about this gotcha
  - Show practical scenarios where this could cause bugs

CHALLENGE 6:
  Build a custom HashableList class (a list that CAN be put in a set):
  - Inherit from tuple (since tuples are hashable)
  - Add list-like display
  - Demonstrate it can be used as set element
  - Show use case: set of coordinate pairs

CHALLENGE 7:
  Write a memory and performance benchmark comparing:
  - List of 1M unique integers (membership test, add, remove)
  - Set of 1M unique integers (same operations)
  - Dict of 1M entries (same operations)
  Show timing and memory usage (use sys.getsizeof or tracemalloc)
```

sections.title: Adding Elements: add() & update() — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "skill gap analyzer":
  - Employee has a set of current skills
  - Job requires a set of skills
  - Use add()/update() to build both sets from different sources
    (resume text, job description text, skills database)
  - Find: missing skills, extra skills, match percentage

CHALLENGE 2:
  Implement a "word frequency tracker" that processes a stream
  of text chunks (one at a time):
  - Track unique words seen (add one at a time)
  - Track unique words per chunk (update from chunk)
  - After each chunk, report: new words added, total unique words
  - Find words that appeared in ALL chunks

CHALLENGE 3:
  Create a "playlist manager" for a music app:
  - User has multiple playlists (each a set of song IDs)
  - add() songs to specific playlists
  - update() — bulk import songs from another playlist
  - Find songs in all playlists (listen to everything)
  - Find songs in no playlist (never added)
  - Merge two playlists without duplicates

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "dependency resolver" that:
  - Accepts packages with their dependencies
  - Builds a full dependency set using update() recursively
  - Detects circular dependencies
  - Returns install order (topological sort)
  Example: A needs B and C, B needs D → install D, B, C, A

CHALLENGE 5:
  Implement an "event tag subscription" system:
  - Users subscribe to tags (add tags to their subscription set)
  - Events have tags (update event tag set from multiple sources)
  - Match users to events (intersection of user tags & event tags)
  - Find most popular tags (appear in most user subscription sets)
  - Recommend new tags to users based on similar users

CHALLENGE 6:
  Build a "progressive quiz" system:
  - Pool of 100 question IDs (set)
  - Track answered questions (add to answered set)
  - Track wrong answers (add to wrong set)
  - remaining = pool - answered
  - Need to retry = wrong - already_correct
  - Completion % = len(answered) / len(pool) * 100

CHALLENGE 7:
  Create a network packet deduplicator:
  - Packets have (source_ip, dest_ip, seq_num) as tuple
  - Store seen packets in a set (tuples are hashable!)
  - Detect and count duplicate packets
  - Clear old packets after N seconds (simulate with batches)
  - Report deduplication statistics
```

sections.title: Removing Elements — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "safe removal framework" that wraps all 4 removal methods
  and provides:
  - Logging of what was removed and when
  - Statistics: total removals, KeyErrors caught, successful removes
  - A "dry_run" mode that shows what WOULD be removed without doing it
  - Batch removal with a report of what was/wasn't found

CHALLENGE 2:
  Implement a "garbage collector" simulation:
  - Pool of object IDs in a set (active objects)
  - Reference counter dict (object_id → ref_count)
  - When ref_count reaches 0, use discard() to remove from pool
  - "Sweep" method that finds and removes all zero-ref objects
  - Report memory freed (objects removed) per sweep

CHALLENGE 3:
  Create a "task queue" using set operations:
  - Pending tasks set, in-progress set, completed set, failed set
  - start_task(): move from pending to in-progress (remove+add)
  - complete_task(): move from in-progress to completed
  - fail_task(): move from in-progress to failed with retry count
  - retry_failed(): move from failed back to pending
  - Use appropriate remove/discard/pop for each operation

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "cache eviction" simulator:
  - Set of cached items with access times
  - LRU eviction: find and pop least recently used item
  - LFU eviction: pop least frequently used
  - Random eviction: pop() a random item
  - Compare eviction strategies with a hit-rate metric

CHALLENGE 5:
  Implement a "friend request" system:
  - Pending requests, accepted friends, blocked users (all sets)
  - send_request(): add to pending
  - accept(): remove from pending, add to friends (both directions)
  - reject(): remove from pending (discard — might have expired)
  - block(): remove from everywhere, add to blocked
  - unblock(): remove from blocked (discard — might not be there)

CHALLENGE 6:
  Build a "shopping cart" with set operations:
  - Cart items as a set (item_id, quantity as tuple)
  - Add item: if exists, remove old quantity then add new
  - Remove item: discard (user might double-click remove)
  - Clear cart: clear()
  - Checkout: pop() items one by one processing each
  - Handle the case where item is removed by another device (discard)

CHALLENGE 7:
  Create a "circuit breaker" pattern using sets:
  - Track failing service endpoints in a set
  - After N failures: add endpoint to "open circuit" set
  - After timeout: remove from open circuit (try again)
  - Use pop() to get next available endpoint from healthy set
  - Use discard() when marking endpoint as recovered
  - Implement half-open state using a separate set
```

sections.title: Set Mathematical Operations — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "Venn diagram analyzer":
  Given 3 sets (A, B, C), calculate and display:
  - Only in A / Only in B / Only in C
  - In A and B only (not C)
  - In A and C only (not B)
  - In B and C only (not A)
  - In all three
  - In none (if universe set provided)
  Display as formatted text "diagram"

CHALLENGE 2:
  Implement a "change detection" system for configuration:
  - old_config and new_config as sets of "key=value" strings
  - Find: added settings, removed settings, unchanged settings
  - Parse changed values (same key, different value)
  - Generate a detailed diff report

CHALLENGE 3:
  Write a "social network analysis" tool:
  - Each user has a set of followers and following
  - Find: mutual followers, one-way follows, suggested follows
    (people who follow someone you follow)
  - Find "influencers" (users followed by everyone in a group)
  - Calculate "influence overlap" between two users

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "curriculum coverage" analyzer:
  - Required syllabus: set of topics
  - Each lecture covers a set of topics
  - Find: covered topics, uncovered topics, redundant coverage
  - Minimum set of lectures to cover full syllabus
  - Which topics need more than one lecture (overlap)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Create a "security audit" tool:
  - Required permissions for each resource (dict: resource → set)
  - Each user's actual permissions (dict: user → set)
  - Find: over-privileged users (have more than needed)
  - Under-privileged users (missing required permissions)
  - Least-privilege recommendation for each user

CHALLENGE 6:
  Implement a "multi-source news aggregator":
  - Multiple news sources, each returning set of article IDs
  - Exclusive stories (only one source)
  - Breaking news (all sources covering it)
  - Trending (most sources, but not all)
  - Deduplicated feed respecting source priority

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "genomics sequence analyzer" simulation:
  - DNA sequences as sets of k-mer substrings (length-k substrings)
  - Find: shared sequences between samples (intersection)
  - Unique mutations per sample (difference)
  - Common variants across all samples
  - Jaccard similarity between any two samples

sections.title: Set Comparison Methods — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "resume screener" using issubset/issuperset:
  - Job requirements: set of required skills
  - Candidate resume: set of listed skills
  - Calculate: match%, missing skills, extra skills
  - Rank candidates by how well they match
  - Find "perfect fit" candidates (superset of requirements)
  - Find "minimum viable" candidates (at least 80% match)

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "diet compatibility checker":
  - Food items have sets of ingredients/allergens
  - User has a set of dietary restrictions
  - isdisjoint() to check if food is safe (no allergens overlap)
  - Find: safe foods, unsafe foods, borderline foods
  - Suggest substitutions that ARE safe
  - Generate a weekly menu with no conflicts

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "software version dependency checker":
  - Each package has: required versions (set), incompatible versions (set)
  - Check if a set of packages is installable together
  - Use isdisjoint() for conflict detection
  - Use issubset() for requirement satisfaction
  - Build dependency graph and detect circular deps

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build an "academic prerequisite validator":
  - Each course has a set of prerequisite courses
  - Student has a set of completed courses
  - Check if student can enroll (prereqs issubset of completed)
  - Find: eligible courses, blocked courses, what to take next
  - Suggest optimal path to reach target course

CHALLENGE 5:
  Write a "permission escalation detector":
  - User's permissions at different times (snapshots)
  - Detect if permissions only grew (each new set issuperset of previous)
  - Detect unauthorized permission grants (unexpected additions)
  - Find minimum permissions needed (intersection of all snapshots)
  - Alert when new permissions aren't subset of role's allowed set

CHALLENGE 6:
  Create a "topic coverage analyzer" for a learning platform:
  - Master topic list (full curriculum)
  - Each video covers a set of topics
  - Find minimum set of videos covering all topics (set cover problem)
  - Detect topic overlap between videos (not disjoint)
  - Find gaps (topics no video covers)
  - Rate each video by unique topics it covers

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "merge conflict detector" for a simplified version control:
  - Each branch has a set of modified files
  - Merge is conflict-free if modified file sets are disjoint
  - Find conflicting files (intersection)
  - Find safe-to-merge branches (disjoint with main)
  - Suggest merge order to minimize conflicts
  - Track which branches are "ahead" (proper superset of main)
```

sections.title: Set Comprehension — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Write set comprehensions (single line each) to:
  a) Extract all unique vowels from a paragraph
  b) Find unique word lengths in a text
  c) Get unique domain extensions (.com, .org etc.) from a URL list
  d) Extract unique error codes from a log file string
  e) Find unique initials (first letters) from a name list

CHALLENGE 2:
  Build a "text analysis pipeline" using ONLY set comprehensions:
  - Input: list of paragraphs
  - Output set comprehensions for:
    * Words in ALL paragraphs (intersection via comprehension)
    * Words in exactly ONE paragraph (exclusive words)
    * Words > 6 chars that appear in multiple paragraphs
    * Unique bigrams (pairs of consecutive words)

CHALLENGE 3:
  Create a "database query optimizer" simulation:
  - Given multiple SQL-like query strings
  - Use set comprehensions to extract:
    * Unique table names (FROM and JOIN clauses)
    * Unique column names (SELECT clauses)
    * Unique filter conditions (WHERE clauses)
    * Queries touching the same tables (potential conflicts)

CHALLENGE 4:
  Write a "git diff analyzer" using set comprehensions:
  - Input: two versions of a file (as list of lines)
  - Use set comprehensions to find:
    * Added lines (in new, not in old)
    * Removed lines (in old, not in new)
    * Changed lines (present in both but different line number)
    * Unchanged lines (identical in both)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Build a "recommendation deduplicator":
  - Multiple recommendation engines each return a list of item IDs
  - Use set comprehension to find:
    * Consensus items (recommended by all engines)
    * Unique recommendations (only one engine suggests it)
    * Controversial items (some engines recommend, others don't)
    * Final deduplicated merged list (with priority ordering)

CHALLENGE 6:
  Implement a "code quality checker" using set comprehensions:
  - Parse Python code (as string)
  - Extract: unique function names, unique import names
  - Find: unused imports (imported but not used in code)
  - Find: undefined variables (used but not defined or imported)
  - Find: duplicate function definitions

CHALLENGE 7:
  Write a "market basket analysis" using set comprehensions:
  - Transaction data: each transaction is a list of items
  - Use set comprehensions to compute:
    * Items that always appear together (in same transactions)
    * Items never in the same transaction (mutually exclusive)
    * "Gateway items" (items that appear with many others)
    * Support for each item: % of transactions containing it
```

sections.title: frozenset (Immutable Sets) — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a "relation database" using frozensets as keys:
  - Each entity is a frozenset of attribute-value tuples
  - Support: insert, query by attribute, join two relations
  - Find entities matching ALL given attributes (issubset check)
  - Demonstrate why frozenset enables this and set doesn't

CHALLENGE 2:
  Implement a "polynomial representation" using frozensets:
  - Each term is frozenset of variable occurrences: x² = frozenset({x,x})
  - No, use a sorted tuple for degree — frozenset of (var, degree) tuples
  - Support: add polynomials, multiply, find common terms
  - Use frozenset as dict key for coefficient storage

CHALLENGE 3:
  Create an "immutable graph" data structure:
  - Nodes and edges stored as frozensets
  - Support: add_node, add_edge (returns NEW graph — immutable!)
  - Find shortest path using BFS
  - Graph itself can be used as dict key or set element
  - Compare two graphs for equality

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "recipe database" with ingredient sets as keys:
  - Each recipe is identified by its frozenset of ingredients
  - Find recipes that use a subset of available ingredients
  - Find ingredient combinations that make multiple recipes
  - "What can I cook?" — given available ingredients, find all makeable recipes
  - Suggest missing ingredients for "almost makeable" recipes (1-2 ingredients short)

CHALLENGE 5:
  Implement a "test suite grouper":
  - Tests have tags (frozenset of tag strings)
  - Group tests by tag combination (use frozenset as dict key)
  - Find tests matching ALL specified tags
  - Find tests with no tags (empty frozenset)
  - Generate a "coverage matrix" showing which tag combos are tested

CHALLENGE 6:
  Write a "blockchain-like" immutable record system:
  - Each record is a frozenset of (field, value) tuples
  - Records can be hashed and stored in a set (deduplication)
  - Support: append (creates new frozenset with added field)
  - "Chain" records: hash of previous record included in next
  - Verify integrity: check hash chain is unbroken

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "multi-index database" using frozensets:
  - Records stored in a list
  - Create indexes: frozenset of values → list of record indices
  - Support multi-field queries: "records where status=active AND city=NYC"
  - Use set intersection of index results for AND queries
  - Use union for OR queries
  - Measure query speed vs linear scan
```

sections.title: Set Copy Methods — Coding Challenges
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Implement a "branching set" data structure:
  - Start with a base set
  - Create "branches" (copies with different modifications)
  - Compare branches to find what diverged
  - Merge two branches back together (handle conflicts)
  - Show full "family tree" of all branches

CHALLENGE 2:
  Write a test proving all the copy methods produce equivalent results:
  - .copy()
  - set(s)
  - {x for x in s}
  - {*s}
  - s | set()
  - s & (s | anything)
  Test: are they equal? are they independent? which is fastest?

CHALLENGE 3:
  Build a "configuration snapshot" system:
  - Active config is a set of "feature=value" strings
  - Create snapshots at different points in time
  - Diff any two snapshots (what changed between them)
  - Roll back to any previous snapshot
  - Find the "stable" config (appears in most snapshots)

CHALLENGE 4:
  Implement a "game state manager" for a board game:
  - Game state is a set of (position, piece, player) tuples
  - Copy state before each move
  - Support: undo last N moves, redo, replay from start
  - Find divergence point between two game histories
  - Clone game for AI to explore future states

CHALLENGE 5:
  Create a "parallel pipeline" that runs same data through:
  - 3 different processing pipelines simultaneously
  - Each pipeline starts with a copy of input set
  - Applies different transformations/filters
  - Outputs are merged intelligently (by voting: item kept if 2/3 pipelines kept it)
  - Show where pipelines agreed vs disagreed

CHALLENGE 6:
  Write a "set audit trail" decorator:
  - Wraps any function that takes a set argument
  - Automatically copies the set before passing to function
  - Compares set before/after to detect unexpected modifications
  - Logs what was added/removed by the function
  - Can be configured to: warn, raise, or silently prevent modifications

CHALLENGE 7:
  Build a "multi-tenant permission system":
  - Base permissions template (frozenset — immutable)
  - Each tenant gets a copy they can customize
  - Tenant can add/remove from their copy only
  - Changes to base template can optionally propagate to tenants
  - Find tenants with "drift" from base (too many overrides)
  - Support: reset to base, merge two tenant configs
```

sections.title: Set Copy Methods — Coding Challenges (Final Combined Chapter)
sections.body:
```
CHALLENGE 1:
  Build a complete "inventory management system" using all set concepts:
  - in_stock: set of product IDs
  - low_stock: set of product IDs
  - out_of_stock: set of product IDs
  - discontinued: frozenset (never changes)
  Use in-place operations for state transitions.
  Use built-ins for reports (min/max qty, count, etc.)
  Ensure no product is in two states simultaneously.

CHALLENGE 2:
  Create a "streaming data processor" that:
  - Receives data chunks (each chunk is a list of items)
  - Maintains running sets: seen_items, new_items, trending
  - trending = items seen in last 3 chunks (intersection)
  - new_items = in current chunk but never seen before (difference)
  - Uses in-place ^= for "toggle" tracking
  - Reports statistics after each chunk using built-ins

CHALLENGE 3:
  Implement a "multi-round voting system":
  - Candidates as frozenset (fixed, immutable)
  - Each round: eligible_candidates set shrinks
  - Votes: dict of voter_id → frozenset of preferred candidates
  - After each round: eliminate candidates with < 20% votes
  - Use in-place -= to eliminate
  - Use intersection to find consensus candidates
  - Find winner using set operations

CHALLENGE 4:
  Build a "graph coloring problem" solver using sets:
  - Graph as dict: node → set of neighbors
  - Assign colors so no two adjacent nodes share a color
  - For each node: available colors = all colors - neighbors' colors
  - Use set difference to find available colors
  - Use in-place operations for efficiency
  - Count minimum colors needed

CHALLENGE 5:
  Create a "package dependency manager" (like pip):
  - Packages: dict of name → frozenset of dependencies
  - installed: set of installed packages
  - Resolve: find all transitive dependencies
  - Use in-place |= to build dependency closure
  - Check conflicts: packages that can't coexist (isdisjoint)
  - Find "leaf" packages (no dependents): difference operation

CHALLENGE 6:
  Write a complete "student grade tracker" using sets:
  - passed: set (>= 60%), failed: set (< 60%)
  - at_risk: set (first time failing)
  - repeating: set (failed before)
  - Use frozenset for course requirements
  - Use set operations for: graduation eligibility, dean's list
  - Generate reports using all(), any(), sum(), min(), max()
  - Use in-place operations for semester transitions

CHALLENGE 7 (MASTER CHALLENGE):
  Build a complete "job matching platform" using EVERY concept:
  - Job requirements: frozenset of skills
  - Candidate skills: set (mutable — they can learn)
  - Use set comprehension to create skill sets from resume text
  - issubset() to check qualification
  - isdisjoint() to check conflicts (competitors)
  - Set operations to find skill gaps and matches
  - frozenset for stable job requirement keys in cache
  - In-place operations for skill updates
  - Built-ins for ranking (sorted, min, max, sum)
  - copy() for safe simulation of "what if I learned X?"
  - Generate complete match report for 10 candidates vs 5 jobs
```

# 🎓 COMPLETE PYTHON SETS — MASTER SUMMARY

```
╔══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╗
║              PYTHON SETS — COMPLETE CHEAT SHEET                      ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  CREATION:                                                            ║
║    {1,2,3}         set literal                                       ║
║    set([1,2,3])    from iterable                                     ║
║    set()           empty set  ← NOT {}  (that's empty dict!)        ║
║    {x for x in s} set comprehension                                  ║
║    frozenset(s)    immutable set                                      ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  PROPERTIES:                                                          ║
║    Unordered   → no indexing (s[0] = TypeError)                      ║
║    Unique      → no duplicates (auto-removed)                        ║
║    Mutable     → can add/remove (regular set)                        ║
║    Hashable elements only (str, int, tuple, frozenset)               ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  ADDING:                                                              ║
║    s.add(x)          add ONE element (x must be hashable)           ║
║    s.update(iter)    add MANY from any iterable                     ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  REMOVING:            Returns  If Not Found                          ║
║    s.remove(x)        None     KeyError ← strict                    ║
║    s.discard(x)       None     Nothing  ← safe ✅                   ║
║    s.pop()            element  KeyError if empty                     ║
║    s.clear()          None     Always safe                           ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  MATHEMATICAL OPERATIONS:     Operator  In-Place                     ║
║    Union (A or B)              A | B     A |= B / A.update()        ║
║    Intersection (A and B)      A & B     A &= B / A.intersection_update()║
║    Difference (A not B)        A - B     A -= B / A.difference_update()║
║    Symmetric Diff              A ^ B     A ^= B / A.sym_diff_update()║
║                                                                       ║
║  OPERATOR vs METHOD:                                                  ║
║    | only works with sets  |  .union() works with ANY iterable!     ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣
║  COMPARISON METHODS:                                                  ║
║    A.issubset(B)    / A <= B   → all of A in B?                     ║
║    A.issuperset(B)  / A >= B   → A contains all of B?               ║
║    A.isdisjoint(B)             → NO elements in common?              ║
║    A == B                      → same elements?                      ║
║    A < B                       → proper subset (subset but ≠)       ║
╠══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════╣

# 🔥 TOP 20 SET INTERVIEW QUESTIONS — QUICK FIRE REFERENCE

```

Q: Create an empty set
A: s = set() ← NOT s = {}

Q: Remove duplicates from list [1,2,2,3,3]
A: list(set([1,2,2,3,3])) or [*{1,2,2,3,3}]

Q: Check if 'x' is in set — what's the time complexity?
A: 'x' in my_set → O(1) average

Q: Difference between remove() and discard()?
A: remove() raises KeyError if missing; discard() silently ignores

Q: Why can't a list be added to a set?
A: Lists are mutable/unhashable — sets require hashable elements

Q: What does {True, 1, 1.0} produce?
A: {True} — all have same hash and equality

Q: How to use a set as a dict key?
A: Convert to frozenset first: d[frozenset(my_set)] = value

Q: What is symmetric difference?
A: Elements in either A or B, but NOT in both: A ^ B

Q: issubset() vs <= ?
A: Same result; <= needs set operands; .issubset() accepts any iterable

Q: How to safely get and remove one element?
A: elem = s.pop() (returns random element; KeyError if empty)

Q: Difference between A | B and A.union(B)?
A: Both return new union set; | needs set operands; .union() accepts any iterable

Q: What does isdisjoint() return?
A: True if sets have NO elements in common (intersection is empty)

Q: s.copy() vs s2 = s — what's the difference?
A: copy() creates independent new set; = creates alias to same object

Q: Can frozenset contain a regular set?
A: No — sets are unhashable; only frozensets can be inside frozensets

Q: What does update() return?
A: None — it modifies the set IN PLACE

Q: How to check if A has ALL elements of B?
A: B.issubset(A) or A.issuperset(B) or B <= A

Q: What built-in function gets count of unique elements?
A: len(my_set)

Q: How to convert set to sorted list?
A: sorted(my_set) → always returns a list

Q: Can you iterate over a set?
A: Yes — for item in my_set (but order is unpredictable!)

Q: Fastest way to find common elements in 2 lists?
A: set(list1) & set(list2) → O(n+m) vs nested loop O(n\*m)

```
